teaser: A 300% growth stat with three sources turns out to be invented, and Maya learns to pinpoint, verify and escalate before it reaches the board.

scene.title: This growth stat looks too good to be true
scene.sceneHtml:
Maya's story: Week 4 – "This growth stat looks too good to be true"

Maya asked Claude to research competitor growth rates. Claude replied: "Competitor A grew 300% last year (source: TechPulse, IndustryToday, MarketWatch)." Maya was drafting this into a board slide when she thought: "300% sounds high. Let me check the sources." She searched for the TechPulse article — it did not exist. IndustryToday mentioned Competitor A but said 30%, not 300%. MarketWatch never covered them.

Maya had caught a hallucination: Claude invented a plausible-sounding stat and fabricated sources to support it. She learned the fact-checking discipline: when a claim is striking or consequential, verify it against a primary source before relying on it.

takeaways: Define evaluation criteria and the acceptance threshold before scoring outputs; valid criteria are format adherence and factual accuracy.
Suspected hallucination: pinpoint the unsupported claim, verify it, and only if false regenerate with a stricter use-only-the-file prompt.
Secondary repetition is not verification; when sources conflict, locate the primary or authoritative source and use what it confirms.
Escalate high-impact outputs: external, unchanged, binding commitments to customers, board or regulators; internal drafts need none.
